Fact checks›Property tax

The claim

Every dollar of the increase goes to public safety

“Every dollar of the increase goes straight to public safety.”

The city's own claim, not one aimed at it. Seen: City messaging, quoted back to the council at the August 6 hearing.

Our finding Accurate, but incomplete

True as far as it goes, and it leaves out something that changes the picture.

True in the schedule's own terms: the levy is smaller than the Sheriff's contract, so there is no second dollar to allocate. What it left out is that the money largely replaces sales tax already paying that contract, and frees the sales tax for other things.

The numbers

Sheriff's contractthe affected budget on the schedule$9,798,139
Rise in the contractover the no-change budget$1,507,939
Raised at 0.000900leaving ≈$4.61M on sales tax≈$5.19M

What’s true

The statutory impact schedule names the Sheriff's contract as the affected budget and puts it at $9,798,139: the same figure, to the dollar, as the proposed property tax revenue. Designed that way, the levy covers the contract and nothing else.

What it leaves out

What actually changes is which pot pays. Property tax takes over a contract sales tax had been subsidizing, and the freed sales tax goes to other city spending: parks, roads, staff. That is a defensible policy and it is not what "every dollar goes to public safety" conveys, which is why residents who did the subtraction, $6.74 million noticed against a $1.5 million rise in the contract, concluded they had been lied to.

More detail

At the rate finally adopted the gap runs the other way and is larger. 0.000900 raises about $5.19 million against a contract of $9,798,139, so roughly $4.61 million of the Sheriff's contract still comes out of sales tax, four times what the repealed rate would have left short.

Where this comes from

Every finding here is drawn from an open-meeting recording or a published document. Check it yourself.
